newsitem.title: INDIA: TEXT-India statement on income tax panel report.
newsitem.headline: TEXT-India statement on income tax panel report.

text.p: Following is a statement issued by the Indian government on Wednesday on the report of an expert committee set up to suggest changes in the income tax structure:

"The goverment of India had constituted an Expert Group to examine the existing income-tax structure and to suggest changes that have become necessary particularly in the light of the new economic policy and tax reforms.

The Group consisted of Dr Amaresh Bagchi, former director, National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, Mr. V.U. Eradi, former member, Central Board of Direct Taxes, Mr. Ramaiah, former secretary, legislative department, Ministry of Law, Mr K. Subramaniam, member, Central Board of Direct Taxes, Mr. H.P. Ranina, advocate, Supreme Court, Mr. T.S. Vishwanath, the then president of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, Mr. S.D. Kapila, commissioner of income tax, Miss M.H. Kherewala, director, management and services, income tax department and Mr. P.K. Saha, deputy commissioner of income tax. MR. K. Subramaniam was nominated as convenor of the Group.
The Group submitted its report to the Finance Minister on February 14, 1997.

While presenting the central government's budget for 1997/98, the Finance Minister had promised in his speech to place a copy of the report in the library of the parliament. Accordingly, copies of the report have been placed in the library of the parliament.
The salient features of the report are given below.

1) The plethora of tax exemptions and deductions should be phased out. The Group states "tax preferences inevitably open up loopholes which are exploited more by resourceful taxpayers and in order to plug them, anti-avoidance provisions are introduced in the law. The end result is the regime of tax laws that are complicated beyond the comphrension of most tax payers and even tax specialists." The Group has favoured simple and intelligible tax laws coupled with reasonable rates of tax. In the context of creating an environment for better tax compliance, the Group has sought to do away with complexities which result in wasteful exercises in setting up tax avoidance schemes. It has also att

2) The Group recommends that the financial year should be continued as the uniform accounting year for all tax payers and with a view to overcoming any confusion in the mind of the average tax payer on the point of the previous year and assessment year, only one expression should be used i.e. the financial year.

3) The Group has favoured deletion of the large number of exemptions from Section 10 of the Income Tax Act. It has also been suggested that institutions for educational and medical purposes etc which are presently exempt under Section 10 and are not subject to any monitoring should be brought within the mainstream of the provisions relating to the charitable institutions. They should be required to get their accounts audited and submit returns with a view to ensuring that the funds are utilised for specific purposes. The Group has not favoured exemption of income from business activities of such institutions except where the activity is integral to achieving the main objects of instituti

4) The group has recommended retention of the present system of taxing income under the heads of income specified in the Act. In regard to salaries, the main recommendation is that the perquisites should be computed at a fixed percentage of the salary and the provision to this effect should be included in the Act. As regards income from house property, the Group is of the view that the concept of annual value should be dispensed with and rental income should be taxed on receipt basis. Further, it is proposed to treat as rent 15 percent per annum as imputed interest on interest free or concessional interest bearing deposits in excess of six months received from the tenant.

The provisions relating to profits and gains of business and profession have been rationalised. The basic recommendation is that all expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for business purposes should be allowed. Therefore the group has recommended the removal of provision making artificial disallowance of business expenses on travelling, maintenence of guest houses, entertainment, etc.

Contribution to employees' welfare funds will be allowed provided the funds invest in prescribed securities. Provision relating to amortisation of preliminary expenses, technical knowhow and prospecting expenses for minerals have been simplified. Similarly provision relating to treatment of gain or loss arising from foreign exchange have been simplified with a view to treating them on revenue account in the year of actual payment realisation.

In regard to provisions relating to depreciation allowance, the group has suggested that the number of blocks of assets which is presently eight should be reduced to four with the rates of depreciation varying from a minimum of 10 percent to a maximum of 50 percent. It is also suggested that all intangible assets like patent rights, copyrights, etc. should constitute a block of assets which would be eligible for depreciation at the general rate of 25 percent applicable to plant and machinery. Further, there should be no time limit on carry-forward of unabsorbed depreciation. In regard to the assessment of professional income, it is suggested that there should be a presumptive rate of ded
5) In regard to taxation of capital assets, the recommendations of the group are:

A) In regard to computation of capital gains on transfer of immovable properties, the valuation of the property on the designated date (presently 1-4-81) has led a large number of disputes. Further, section 54 to 54EB provde for large number of tax shelters which are also sometimes difficult to comply with. It is proposed that for assets other than financial assets, held for more than eight years, sixty percent of the sale proceeds will be deemed to be the cost of acquisition. For assets held for less than 8 years but more than 3 years, fifty percent of the sale proceeds will be deemed to be the cost of acquisition. A further deduction of the fifty percent of the gains would be allowed a
An individual will be free to use the balance 93 percent for any purpose and there will be no need for providing any exemption provisions.

B) In regard to scheme for taxing capital gains on financial assets, it is proposed to constitute a block of such assets and the assessee will have the option either to furnish actual indexed cost of each asset or to substitute the market value of the entire holding of the financial asset prevailing on 31st March 1990.

As long as the value of the block is positive, no tax is attracted. Even if the value goes into the negative and the assessee replenishes the block by purchasing some other assets and thus bringing the value of the block to a positive figure, there would be no capital gains.
The value of the block will be reduced by the sale proceeds and increased by the purchase price as and when the assets are sold or purchased.

Financial assets will include all securities including debentures and bonds which are freely tradeable. Any bond which is freely tradeable and the cummulative interest is payable only on maturity, would also be considered to be a financial asset. In other words, interest received on maturity of Deep Discount Bonds would be taxable to capital gains.
C) The scheme would also apply to transactions like slump rate by companies.
D) With a view to enabling business re-organisations, it is proposed that transactions between a holding company and its 51 percent subsidiary would not be subjected to capital gains.
E) Any proprietary concern or a partnership firm converting into a company would not be subjected to capital gains.

F) With a view to discouraging the widespread practice of understating consideration in the sale deed, it is proposed that assessing officer will have the power to substitute the value on the basis of which stamp duty is paid.

6) A).Major changes have been suggested in regard to taxation of dividend. It is proposed that instead of taxing dividend in the hands of the shareholders, a company should be directly taxed on the profits distributed by it.
The rate of tax is proposed to be ten percent of the profit distributed.

As regards the corporates which distribute profit of an ammount exceeding the amount of total income on which it was assessed for the immediately preceding financial year, the rate of tax would be twenty percent, on such excess amount. This would take care of zero tax companies distributing dividend.
It is also proposed that the dividend distributed by mutual funds should be taxed at the rate of ten percent at the point of distribution. The unit holders would therefore not be taxed.

B) It is also suggested that the provisions of section 115JA (Minimum Alternate Tax) should be deleted keeping in view the scheme of taxation of dividend proposed by the group. 7) A) The group has suggested that relief on foreign exchange earning through exports should be at a fixed percentage of the foreign exchange repatriated to India. As a consequence, sections 10A and 10B will be deleted.

b) Section 88 should be deleted and should be substituted by a new provision akin to the old Section 80C. The assessee will be eligible to a deduction at the rate of 100 percent up to a ceiling of 100,000 rupees on savings in prescribed investments.

8).A special provision with a view to combating tax avoidance schemes is proposed to be enacted. The provision is on the lines of similar provisions already existing in the tax statues of various countries, like U.K., Australia, Malaysia and Singapore.

9) The group has also suggested streamlining of assessment procedures, the main recommendation being the deletion of the existing provisions of sub-section(1)(a) and (1A) of section 143 to be substituted by a simple provision whereby the assessing officer will either accept the return and intimate the same or take it up for scrutiny under section 143(3).

10) The appellate procedure is proposed to be overhauled. The existing reference procedure is proposed to be substituted by a direct appeal to high court on the lines similar to the provisions of Civil Procedure Code. This will speed up the finalisation of tax liability.

It is also proposed to constitute a college of commissioners whose order on the dispute between the assessee and the department will be final both on the assessee and the department. This will be at the option of the assessee who will give an undertaking that he will not take recourse to the existing appellate procedure.
11) The group has recommended the deletion of the provisions relating to pre-emptive purchase of property under Chapter XX-C of the Income-tax Act.
12) The provisions relating to penalties and prosecutions have also been streamlined in the report.
13).An important recommendation of the group is deletion of Section 64 which provides for clubbing of income of spouses and minors.
